Black rockfish (Sebastes inermis) reach an asymptotic body length of 35.9 cm [Li = 35.9 cm], a maximum size that distinguishes them from smaller congeners inhabiting the same rocky reef ecosystems along the Japanese archipelago. The total length at which this species attains puberty is 16 cm [Lp = 16 cm], a relatively modest size threshold compared to the ultimate length. This early onset of gonadal maturation, occurring at just under half the maximum length, is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output in a variable coastal environment. As a viviparous teleost, females retain fertilised eggs internally, and the developing yolk-sac larvae are sustained by endogenous reserves until parturition. The initial wet mass of each newly released prolarva has been estimated at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a tiny but remarkably consistent size that reflects the extreme efficiency of yolk provisioning in this genus. This mass corresponds to an oocyte diameter of approximately 0.8 mm prior to fertilisation, though the viviparous mode of development means that free-swimming larvae emerge at a more advanced developmental stage than do the pelagic eggs of most other scorpionfishes.

Field surveys and laboratory rearing studies have provided detailed information on the growth trajectory and reproductive allocation of S. inermis. Using the established length-weight relationship for the species, the predicted wet weight at the onset of puberty is 55.7 grams [Wwp = 55.7 grams], a body mass that suffices for the initiation of vitellogenesis and the subsequent brooding of developing embryos. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult, corresponding to the maximum length, is approximately 640 grams [Wwi = approximately 640 grams], representing more than a tenfold increase in somatic mass from the pubertal stage. This considerable scope for post-maturational growth is typical of iteroparous rockfishes, which channel surplus energy into both somatic maintenance and successive reproductive bouts over many years. The length-weight relationship itself, derived from extensive morphometric sampling of wild populations, follows a power function with an exponent near 3.0, indicating near-isometric scaling of body mass with length and reflecting a consistent body shape throughout the adult size range. Such allometric consistency simplifies the estimation of energetic demands and reproductive output across different size classes in population models.

The reproductive biology of S. inermis is characterized by a distinct pattern of copulatory behaviour and internal fertilisation, followed by a prolonged gestation period. Under a stable thermal regime of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C], a typical female produces approximately 170 offspring per parturition event [N_R_i = approximately 170 offspring per parturition event] and completes roughly one spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per year], yielding a modest annual reproductive output compared to many batch-spawning teleosts. This single, synchronized annual brood is an adaptation to seasonal cycles of primary productivity and prey availability in temperate coastal waters. The maximum reproductive rate of the species, reflecting the highest potential fecundity under optimal conditions, is expressed as a combination of brood size and frequency, with the per-event fecundity representing the upper bound of larval production. Gestation proceeds internally as the yolked ova complete embryonic development, and the alevin are extruded as active, free-swimming larvae during late winter or early spring, a timing that coincides with peak zooplankton abundance and maximizes larval survival.

Longevity estimates for S. inermis place the species among the longer-lived members of the Sebastes genus found in the temperate Northwest Pacific. At the same thermal regime of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C], the maximum documented lifespan in wild populations is approximately 40 years [am = approximately 40 years], with the oldest individuals occasionally reaching up to 50 years in less exploited habitats. This extended lifespan, exceeding that of many other coastal scorpionfishes, is linked to a slow pace of life characterized by delayed senescence, low natural mortality after maturity, and a persistent capacity for iterative spawning across multiple decades. The metabolic costs associated with such longevity are met through a diet of benthic invertebrates and small fishes, which provide a steady energy intake throughout the year. Age validation studies using otolith annuli have confirmed that growth slows markedly after the first decade, but individuals continue to gain mass and maintain gonadal function well into their third or fourth decade. This life-history strategy, combining late maturity with high annual survivorship, makes the species particularly sensitive to overfishing, as the removal of older, highly fecund individuals can disproportionately depress population recruitment.

Comparisons with congeneric species highlight the intermediate position of S. inermis in the rockfish life-history continuum. Whereas some deep-dwelling Sebastes species attain ages exceeding 100 years and achieve pubertal lengths well beyond 30 cm, the black rockfish exhibits a more compressed schedule, completing its lifespan at 40 years [am = 40 years] in water temperatures near 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C]. The size at puberty, measured as a total length of 16 cm [Lp = 16 cm], is notably smaller than that of the giant Sebastes species, which may delay maturation until reaching lengths greater than 40 cm. This early maturation likely reflects the selective pressures of a shallow, reef-associated habitat where predation on juveniles is high and the probability of surviving to an advanced age is correspondingly low. The relatively modest ultimate wet weight of 640 grams [Wwi = 640 grams] also places S. inermis in the small-to-medium size range within the genus, consistent with its reliance on cryptic shelter in rock crevices rather than the open-water schooling behaviour of larger pelagic species. Overall, the life-history parameters of the black rockfish describe a species that balances moderate fecundity and extended longevity against the constraints of a structured, near-shore environment.
